title: New GeoServer RCE exploit chain seen in the wild two days after disclosure
raw_text: Attackers have begun probing a chain of five GeoServer vulnerabilities that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, just two days after the open source geospatial server project disclosed the flaws. Security firm watchTowr, which operates a global network of honeypot servers, reported that it observed the probing activity in the early morning hours of Wednesday. Attackers from multiple IP addresses created stored queries on GeoServer instances, checked whether they were created, and deleted them immediately, a technique that confirms a server is vulnerable without delivering a malicious payload. GeoServer is widely used by government agencies, utilities, and large organizations to publish maps and geospatial data, and it has become a recurring target for attackers. The full RCE chain was reported to the project in August by Jonah Burgess, a senior security researcher at Rapid7 who uses the online handle CryptoCat. The GeoServer project shipped fixes in October and early November but only disclosed the vulnerabilities and published advisories for them on Monday. Chained together, the flaws allow an external unauthenticated attacker to bypass security restrictions, read stored secrets, forge an administrator authentication cookie, and ultimately execute code on the underlying host. They affect GeoServer versions 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, and 2.27.6 and earlier. Users are advised to upgrade to the fixed versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 depending on which major release they use. A five-flaw chain According to Burgess’ technical write-up this week, one flaw (CVE-2026-129244) uses an overly long stored-query request to trigger a filesystem error that exposes the server’s data-directory path. A second flaw (CVE-2026-129243) allows attackers to call services with a slash in their names, such as x/WFS, bypassing access rules and letting unprivileged users create and delete stored queries, an action normally reserved for administrators. A saved query can then read files from the server, returning the administrator’s password digest along with a cookie-signing key that ships with the default value “geoserver,” a bug tracked as CVE-2026-120705. That key can then be used to forge an administrator cookie (CVE-2026-129245), and a deserialization bug in the database-backed user service finally allows running code with the privileges of the GeoServer process (CVE-2026-129242). Only the final step results in code execution, and only one of the five flaws, the predictable signing key, is rated as critical. Burgess also published a proof-of-concept exploit for the chain. However, researchers from Eye Security independently found a shorter, three-flaw RCE chain that shares the file-read step but reaches code execution through a different bug tracked as CVE-2026-120704 that was also patched. Eye Security used AI models to find the bugs, and the fact that different researchers found some of the same vulnerabilities (two researchers named McCaulay and Quikko are also credited on some of the flaws) highlights the fact that attackers could use AI to find the flaws as well, especially since patches can serve as blueprints for AI agents . In fact, Eye Security had to consider whether delaying disclosure after patches were released was worth the risk of malicious actors finding them independently in the meantime. “We used AI to find these bugs, and a determined attacker with good models could do the same, especially with the official patch to diff against,” Niels Teusink, a security researcher at Eye Security, wrote this week. “That makes the gap between releasing a fix and publishing details riskier than it used to be.” After the advisories were published, it took less than two days for attackers to start probing the flaws to identify vulnerable servers, likely in preparation for attacks. Over 3,000 GeoServer instances are currently exposed to the internet. GeoServer keeps getting targeted This is not the first time GeoServer has been targeted by attackers. In August , a zero-day SQL injection flaw was exploited before a patch was available , and in December 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ordered US agencies to patch another GeoServer flaw under active exploitation . Upgrading to a patched release resolves the entire chain, but the patches generate a new cookie-signing key that invalidates existing remember-me sessions. Clustered deployments must set a shared GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY so nodes sign cookies with the same key, and since the data directory might have been exposed, administrators should also change their passwords. Where patching cannot happen immediately, GeoServer advises blocking requests whose service value contains a slash, removing the remember-me filter from the web filter chain, and checking the data directory’s wfs/query folders for stored queries not created by a legitimate user.

title: Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
raw_text: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux. The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root. “Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.” Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2. A second patch cycle in a month For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory . PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface. The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.” The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.” Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.” Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained. “It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said. Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug. “The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again. From web shell to root The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds. According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data. The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day. Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said. “A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said. The firewall as a foothold Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue. “A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.” “If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. Asked why the kernel fix took six months to reach PAN-OS, and whether Panorama is affected, Palo Alto said it had “no further information to share beyond what is outlined in the advisory at this time.”

The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root. “Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.” Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score.

title: Broadcom issues fixes for 23 new VMware flaws, three critical
raw_text: Broadcom on Tuesday reported almost two dozen new security vulnerabilities in VMware, adding to a lengthy list of fixes from this month alone. The most serious of the flaws in the current advisory is a vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-123903, assigned a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 (Critical). “A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system,” it said. In a supplemental document accompanying the alert , Broadcom noted that because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing, the advisory comes just two days before the US Thanksgiving holiday, admitting, “this timing is not optimal.” The company said that the advisory covers a total of 23 issues, seven of which are in vCenter: an authentication bypass and three denial-of-service issues in the VMware Directory Service, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS). Seven more are in ESX: a heap out-of-bounds write and a use-after-free in the I/O filter service, an out-of-bounds write in the Extensible Host Controller Interface (XHCI) USB controller, a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a security bypass in the host configuration store, a signature verification bypass, and a denial of service in guest RPC. The remaining flaws affect VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, VMware Tools, and VMware Avi Load Balancer. However, the company noted that the fixes delivered to address the flaws in last week’s advisory resolve some of the issues highlighted in the current batch. “If you applied vCenter 8.0 U3m for VMSA-2026-0009 , including on VCF 5.2.x, you do not need to update vCenter again, but vCenter 9.1.x needs the update in this advisory,” Broadcom said. “ESX was not part of VMSA-2026-0009 and needs the update in this advisory. VMSA-2026-0009 also resolved issues in SDDC Manager, which this advisory does not update. If you have not applied the SDDC Manager update from VMSA-2026-0009, apply it separately. This advisory also includes a VMware Tools update. Updating vCenter and ESX does not update VMware Tools inside virtual machines, so plan that update separately.” It added, “if you have a question about whether you are affected, it is likely that you are and should take action immediately.” Difference of opinion on patching urgency So is this a signal to interrupt the US Thanksgiving holiday to address the flaws? Opinions differ. Tyler Reguly , Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, argued that although a 9.8 score is about as high as they get, the nature of the holes might not merit extreme scheduling. There are three vulnerabilities rated 9.8 in severity listed in the current batch, affecting VMware vCenter and ESX. He pointed out, “neither of these [affected] systems should be present on your external interfaces, so the risk would need to be internal. That means we’re talking about an inside threat or a breach that is already underway. These are important vulnerabilities, so there’s no doubt about that, but they are not so important that anyone should interrupt their holiday weekend.” Reguly suggested a strict interpretation of CISA guidance to support his contention that these patches may not merit emergency response. “If we take a look at CISA BOD-26-04 as our guidance on this, is the service publicly exposed? It shouldn’t be, so let’s say no. Is this vulnerability in the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]? No. Could it be automated? Unknown, so let’s assume yes for safety’s sake,” he said. “A result of No, No, and Yes translates to line 13 on the BOD-26-04 remediation timelines, which allows for 60 days to fix the issue.” He observed that the recent onslaught of vulnerabilities has made us “a bit like Pavlov’s dog:” We’ve been conditioned to react every time we see CVSS 9.8. “This is a dangerous and potentially harmful conditioning that we need to make every effort to break,” he said. “We need to remind ourselves that the severity of a vulnerability does not reflect risk to an organization, just as the bell did not represent food.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, disagreed. He considered the current advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, to be “a big deal because it hits vCenter and ESX, the two systems that run every virtual machine, with flaws that need no password. Skip the patch, and one attacker can take down or take over every virtual machine you run. You are essentially toast. Patch now.” Dickson noted that this batch of alerts contains multiple problematic security issues, which include authentication bypass in vCenter; permitting an attacker with network access to run code on the hypervisor itself; and another bug that lets an administrator inside a virtual machine on Workstation or Fusion run code on the host computer. “Let’s face it: AI loves to chain vulnerabilities,” he said. He is also worried about the large number of VMware patches this month alone, especially those in vCenter. “The frequency of VMware’s vCenter flaws is a concern, as they keep landing in the same place,” he said. “The new flaw is distinct from last week’s. Distinct is not comforting. Three different holes in the same wall is a wall problem.” He pointed out, “The directory service has become vCenter’s Achilles’ heel. This advisory adds three denial-of-service flaws in the same service for good measure.”

title: Check Point security management servers hit in global cyberattack campaign
raw_text: An active intrusion campaign targeting Check Point security management servers has been uncovered, with confirmed attack activity observed between October 17 and November 2, 2026, impacting 22 organizations globally. Tracked by cybersecurity firm GreyNoise as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), the campaign does not appear to be focused on a single region or industry. Impacted organizations span assets across the US, the UK, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, and Australia, across sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. “The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique,” a Check Point spokesperson said. “Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity. The most important action is to install the available updates for CVE-2026-16232. Check Point has already released fixes and detailed mitigation and investigation guidance in its SecureKnowledge advisory.” GreyNoise has not attributed GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group. “An intrusion into a Check Point security management server is particularly serious because it is not just another server in the enterprise network. It effectively acts as the central control point for managing an organisation’s firewall infrastructure and security policies, with highly privileged access,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. He said that depending on the deployment and the level of access obtained, the consequences could extend well beyond the security infrastructure itself, potentially exposing sensitive data and critical business applications and disrupting enterprise operations. Building the relay infrastructure The threat actor operated across 99 IP addresses, primarily routed outbound through ExpressVPN or compromised Check Point devices, generating more than 1,400 network sessions, over 800 command-line artifacts, and over 1,200 created, uploaded, or downloaded files. GreyNoise first observed the actor scanning and exploiting a Rejetto HFS server on October 2, 2026. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returned a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm and thus recover an HFS session cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allowed the attacker to log in as admin without a password. A few minutes later, GreyNoise observed that admin requests with forged session cookies were used to gain control of the server. This led GreyNoise to believe that exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The forged cookie contained “allow_session_ip_change:true”, allowing forged cookies to work from any IP address. On October 5, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server, the research said. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Three days later, on October 8, the threat actor automation check in to the compromised server using the HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Instead of using SSH access right away, on October 19, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. GreyNoise noted that it believes the idea was to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations. As the malware download failed, the threat actor returned with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay the next day. On October 20, the threat actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) for setting up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, which they used to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from a scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point security management server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy. Targeted intrusion Once the compromised server was established as a relay, the actor used it to manage interactions with previously compromised Check Point devices, actively deepening their intrusion against Victim A while conducting bulk actions across 21 other victim organizations. Across the campaign, the operator relied on at least 30 Python scripts, including helpers, launchers, vulnerability probes, and exploit runners. Between October 20 and 26, the attacker had a compromised Victim A asset download and run Chisel in client mode, allowing them to further scan and interact with Victim A’s environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232, the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point management servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix NetScaler , Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter , Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers. Between October 20 and 21, the attacker focused on Victim A, first using exploit.py (CVE-2026-16232) against one Check Point server before scanning a second with spray_portal.py. When that second device failed to report back to the relay box, the actor created pull_.py to steal credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configurations through the first compromised server. The attacker then expanded inside Victim A’s network, running broad port scans with curl, telnet, nmap, and a domain controller probe, followed by targeted exploits against internal Microsoft Netlogon, Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware vCenter servers. They wrapped up this phase by running comb.py,ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py populated with victim-themed usernames and passwords. On October 26, the operation shifted to bulk targeting. The actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers, including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. Results were shipped in a text file to the hop server that contained an incrementing IP order to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via SCP to this exfil folder. Although the task failed on every device, the error logs sent back to the hop server exposed victim IP addresses and revealed an /etc/ld.so.preload reference to /usr/lib/.libproc.so, pointing to a likely implant before activity paused until November 2. GreyNoise suspects the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus including separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting. Securing the management plane Although GreyNoise’s direct visibility into the campaign paused around November 2, 2026, security leaders must still verify whether their environments have been quietly infiltrated. With attackers planting backdoors on breached Check Point servers, CISOs must audit their environments for signs of quiet compromise. To establish whether Check Point infrastructure has been compromised, CISOs and security teams should examine administrative login records for unusual access patterns, including unfamiliar IP addresses, unexpected login times, and unauthorised access added Dhar. They should also look for changes to firewall policies, access-control rules, and configuration files, and thoroughly review system logs, audit trails, and command execution history for suspicious activity. Dhar noted that once there are indications of a compromise, the immediate priority should be to prevent further access and contain the damage. Security teams should restrict access to the management server to authorised administrative systems and isolate confirmed compromised systems while preserving forensic evidence. Unauthorised accounts should be disabled, suspicious SSH keys and access tokens revoked, and identified malicious IP addresses and domains blocked.

title: Prompting AI to be ‘thorough’ can drive sandbox escapes, Anthropic says
raw_text: Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a poorly secured sandbox, Anthropic has found in its latest evaluation. The evaluation, called Siren, gives Claude models routine dev-ops tasks inside deliberately weakened sandboxes and places a “honeypot,” such as a credential, file, or emulated internet service, outside the boundary, Anthropic researchers Oscar O’Rahilly and Darya Kaviani wrote in a blog post . Anthropic tested six Claude models, from Mythos 5 to the 5.5 series, without the safeguards that ship in its products. The tests covered more than 1,700 scenarios in 26 sandboxes built on tools including Docker, gVisor, and QEMU. Most of the weaknesses are misconfigurations modeled on public reports, the company said. Wording mattered more than deadlines Anthropic’s researchers tested different types of instructions, which they called “tempters”. Some increased urgency by introducing deadlines or the consequences of failure. Others encouraged agents to search extensively or gave them broad authority over their machines. “Some tempters give the model broad authority over its own machine. Others tell it to search thoroughly, on that machine or more widely, and list what it checked,” the researchers wrote. Removing deadlines and stated costs of failure changed the rate of reaching outside by no more than about six percentage points, the post said. Removing the wording that asked for thoroughness and asserted authority had a far larger effect, cutting reach rates by 23 to 26 points in five of the six models, the researchers wrote. Claude Mythos 5 was the exception, reaching outside about 90% of the time in every version of the scenarios, the post added. Across the Claude 5.5 models and Claude Mythos 5.2, agents reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios, but misaligned use occurred in only 0.6% to 1.6%. The corresponding misaligned-use rates for the older Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 models were 25.8% and 12.7%, respectively, according to the post. “Siren is designed to make this behavior easy to measure; its rates are not an estimate of how often this behavior happens in real use,” the company wrote. Six rules in the system prompt The first mitigation Anthropic tested was spelling out six sandbox rules in the system prompt. They cover host files, host services, container engine sockets, credentials, network destinations, and anything left running on the host after a task ends. The rules made the models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside, cutting the rate for the newest models to about 2% or less, the researchers wrote. Mythos 5 still reached outside in nearly a quarter of scenarios. Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said no CISO should rely solely on system prompt rules as a control for agents. “It’s like marking your own homework: asking a model to moderate itself is a high-risk approach,” Brown said. Mitigations reduce boundary crossing Anthropic tested three measures to reduce the likelihood of agents reaching outside their sandboxes. The first involved explicitly describing the sandbox, specifying which resources were off-limits, and instructing the model to stop and report if a task required resources it had not been given. This reduced reaching-out rates by 68% to 96%, depending on the model. A tool allowing agents to report sandbox weaknesses rather than exploit them reduced the rate by seven to 33 percentage points. The third measure, auto mode, uses a classifier to check tool calls before execution. In an offline replay of the test episodes, it blocked the first command accessing external material in 96% to 100% of misaligned use cases. It blocked the first command attempting to reach outside in 53% to 84% of boundary-crossing episodes. The mitigations make escape less likely but “don’t fix the sandbox itself,” Anthropic wrote. Brown said enterprises should not rely on AI vendors to secure their own models. Instead, they should encase agents in a governance structure that limits scope and access to what is required and no more, he said. “CISOs may use AI to govern AI, but they must ensure that the governance AI is from a different vendor and has a different model provenance than the one they are governing,” Brown said. Models suspect they are being tested Anthropic also found that models frequently suspected they were being tested. Claude Sonnet 5.5 showed signs of evaluation awareness in 67% of scenarios. Across the four newer models, the rate ranged from 43% to 67%. “With only six models, we can’t tell whether models are more cautious about reaching outside because they suspect they are in a test, or whether the increased eval awareness and the reduced tendency to leave the sandbox are both products of how newer models were trained,” the researchers wrote. Brown said enterprises should not rely on vendor-produced evaluations alone when deciding whether to deploy agents. “Agents are goal-focused and will stop at nothing to achieve their mission,” he said. Organisations should instead deploy agents with “an identified sponsor, a clear scope, an expiry date and an evidential record of what the agent actually did.”

title: Despite doom and gloom headlines, AI attacks are thin on the ground
raw_text: When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology. Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment. And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats. Has that happened? Well, kind of. What CISOs are seeing In the first quarter of 2026, RSAC asked Fortune 1000 CISOs whether they’d seen definitive evidence of AI-powered attack techniques being used against their companies, beyond social engineering, and 44% said yes. “We asked the same question in Q4 of a similar cohort,” says Laura Koetzle, RSAC’s head of community research. According to preliminary results — the survey isn’t complete yet — nearly 58% now say they’ve seen evidence of AI-powered attack techniques. As a result, the majority of CISOs are revamping their vulnerability management programs, according to the forthcoming survey. But they’re not upending how they approach cybersecurity, Koetzle adds. “The same foundational principles still apply.” The main difference today is in speed and quantity, she says. Lincoln Wallen, CTO at Framestore, an Academy Award–winning visual effects company, isn’t turning a blind eye to what AI could be used for by attackers. “We take the potential very seriously,” he says. But he’s taking an old-school approach to dealing with this new threat. “We’re putting a lot of emphasis on cleanliness, hygiene, and patching.” So far, the signs of AI use have been limited to more sophisticated phishing attacks, he says. “They feel anecdotally more well put-together, more convincing, involving many more disparate elements of data,” he says. “That’s the most concrete thing that we’ve seen.” To deal with that, the company has updated its anti-phishing training. Another area that Framestore is investing in is more efficient and prioritized patching and more frequent penetration testing. Enhanced productivity but familiar threats The data seems to support Framestore’s approach, even if the headlines don’t. Last week, headlines quoted Google’s announcement that “ the era of autonomous attacks had arrived ” — a reference to Google’s original blog post teaser to its latest AI Threat Tracker report. But in the actual report , John Hultquist, chief analyst at the Google Threat Intelligence Group, seemed to undercut this top line teaser, saying: “For the most part, attackers aren’t using new groundbreaking methods to break into systems — they are still going after known, unfixed issues, just with much greater speed and scale.” (Google later changed its headline to “ Outpace automated cyber threats with security built for nonstop defense .”) According to Google’s report, the mechanics of intrusion remain the same. Even attackers using new AI-powered attack frameworks are using them to leverage compromised credentials and unpatched systems. It’s the speed and scale at which these frameworks can be used that’s the challenge. In fact, using LLMs can even hurt the attackers, as the frameworks “trade stealth for velocity,” researchers say. The attacks can be “forensically noisy” and can hallucinate non-existent details or targets. “Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don’t.” Or, as Sergej Epp summed up as a takeaway from a recent Cloud Security Alliance CISO huddle call on autonomous attacks, “detecting these attacks is — at least for now — not the hard part. They make a lot of noise, like 1000 interns.” Austin Berglas, managing director and head of cyber operations at Nardello & Co., a global investigations firm, says he’s not seeing AI-discovered zero days or self-replicating AI agents out in the wild. “This is one of those examples that is still in the lab environment,” he says. Most attackers are using AI the way everyone does, he says. “Just like individuals use it for their daily productivity and efficiency, same with the bad actors. They’re able to scale, do it cheaper, do it quicker. And you’re seeing people who typically wouldn’t have the technical chops to do something, who are now able to do it because AI can do the technical side.” The industry is seeing evidence of faster weaponization of vulnerabilities, confirms Gartner analyst John Watts. “Where it starts to have less evidence is for fully autonomous attacks. What happened with Hugging Face is a fully autonomous attack, and that isn’t that common.” How CISOs should respond But if the wave of autonomous attacks and AI-powered malware hasn’t yet fully arrived, what should CISOs do given the reality on the ground? “The feedback that we get from our client base is that they believe there’s a lot of value in using the controls they already have,” Gartner’s Watts says. “The wake-up call for the practitioners is to get busy with the patching,” confirms Paul Webber, an analyst at Software Analyst Cyber Research, adding that security by obscurity is no longer an option. The biggest problem enterprises are facing, he notes, is that they need better automation to handle the increased workload, and the tools aren’t yet where they need to be. “People need more trust in the security tools so they can move from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop towards fully autonomous response,” Webber says. “And that’s going to take some discipline, some standardization, and some proof in the efficacy of the security tools themselves. At the moment, they’re neither built to a specific standard or definition and people are being asked to make purchasing decisions without physical proof that the tools can do what they purport to do.” And, in some ways, the much-lauded defensive AI capabilities can make things worse — such as by exposing legacy vulnerabilities that companies now have to hurry up and patch, on top of their already large backlog. “This is a conversation that we’re actively having right now,” says Christina Powers, partner and cybersecurity consulting leader at West Monroe, a management consulting firm. “We’re working with a mid-sized bank, and they are just completely lost on how to keep up with the number of vulnerabilities that they got,” she says. “They’re sitting on millions of vulnerabilities. They don’t even know where to start. There’s a bit of analysis paralysis that’s happening because there’s so much information coming in.” The tools are improving all the time, Powers says, but she recommends security leaders not to wait for better technology to come along. “If you’re sitting and waiting, you become more of a target because you’re falling behind,” she says.
summary: When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology. Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment. And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats. Has that happened?

title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
raw_text: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries. In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset. The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual. Need to buy time “For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post . “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.” But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said. He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug . Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out. “We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said. Making the infrastructure secure from the start Shirudo combines Cisco’s infrastructure with OpenAI’s frontier models and AI research. It is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which supports the running of small, sandboxed programs inside a Linux kernel without changing source code or loading additional modules. “This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems,” OpenAI explained in its blog post announcing the project . Speaking in their own language, guardian agents investigate and detect flaws and build shields, then test whether they stop the attack, all without disrupting the targeted service. The shields are cryptographically signed and only loaded when verified and deemed safe. Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against safety rules, and kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being added or removed. All this takes place even if attackers have already gained access to a system. Further, self-defending agents can monitor for false positives, performance, and overall system health, and incorporate red-team findings and other feedback as well as signals for continuous improvement. Evidence backing every control travels across the system. The idea, according to Cisco and OpenAI, is to make the infrastructure itself secure by default. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer,” OpenAI wrote in its post. Shirudo in the wild Shirudo has its roots in Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform developed and open-sourced by Isovalent, which was acquired by Cisco in 2024 . It is already incorporated into Cisco’s Live Protect capability. But Tetragon has been rewritten for the agentic era; its previous iteration pointed AI to human-oriented consoles, configuration files, and policy languages. In that workflow, the agent thought in machine code, which was then decoded for humans and processed, then translated back again into machine code. With Shirudo, agents interact in their natural language, which is code. “Agents are different,” Isovalent co-founder Thomas Graf and its chief open source officer Liz Rice noted in a blog post : They are very good at generating code, can absorb huge amounts of context quickly, and “[don’t] mind reverse engineering several million lines of assembly code.” In one controlled testing environment, researchers fed information about the Java4Shell vulnerability into Shirudo, which automatically created a shield against exploitation, generating a mitigation in Java bytecode which was injected into any Java app and added validation on the base64 input to guard against exploit attempts by threat actors. Graf and Rice explained that agent loops can either be tasked to actively search for new vulnerabilities on their own, or work off external sources like newly-available security disclosures. Agents can generate mitigation code, reproduce and validate exploits, and determine the most effective patching measures. This step is repeated until the agent identifies a successful path. The shield is then signed and securely rolled out to vulnerable nodes; it retires when a patch is installed. “This step is continuously monitored and repeated to achieve the highest possible security score while closely monitoring the health of applications,” Graf and Rice explained. It can be designed to be “more or less autonomous.” Once mitigation shields are deployed, the system employs a “hit” count of active exploitation attempts, so that exploits can be investigated on demand. Ultimately, the Shirudo project is only the beginning, Graf and Rice noted, but it already shows “true potential” and the hope is it will continue to evolve in the open source ecosystem. “We believe that building secure infrastructure for the AI era is an industry-scale problem,” they said. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, a permissive open-source software license approved by the Open Source Initiative. This allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute software, including in proprietary or commercial products, with minimal restrictions. Its BPF programs are dual licensed under GPL and BSD. Developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators are encouraged to inspect the code, test outcomes, and contribute to the project’s development. Barrister Karon Monaghan KC has been appointed to conduct an independent review of the UK’s information and data protection regulator, following an internal investigation into its former chief, John Edwards, who resigned after being accused of using “vulgar and highly sexualised language” towards women.

Monaghan – an experienced barrister who has been involved in investigations into sexual harassment at the GMB trade union and the Labour Party’s handling of sexual harassment complaints and antisemitism – is due to report back in the first quarter of next year.

She confirmed today that the Information Commission will not enforce any non-disclosure agreements signed by current and former members of staff at the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), so that there would be no restriction on people speaking, writing or providing documents to the review team.

The review follows complaints by staff of the existence of a wider toxic workplace culture at the ICO, with a staff survey finding that a high proportion had witnessed bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Wayne Parry, national officer at the FDA union for managers and professionals in public service, said there were continuing problems in the workplace, with former staff confirming to Computer Weekly that the ability of the ICO to regulate effectively had been impacted.

“Poor behaviour including bullying remains a significant concern for our members who work at the commission,” he said. “Our recent survey revealed that 65% of participants reported bullying, harassment and discrimination was a serious problem.”

The review will focus on the culture, accountability and governance of the ICO, including examining how complaints are raised, assessed and acted upon, but will not have powers to discipline staff or determine misconduct.

Women were ‘shocked and uncomfortable’

Former technology secretary Liz Kendall wrote on LinkedIn following Edwards’ resignation in the summer that “multiple women shared testimony … on feeling offended, shocked and uncomfortable following interactions with Mr Edwards”.

Current and former staff at the ICO told Computer Weekly in July that it was “inconceivable” that senior leaders at the organisation, including current chief executive Paul Arnold, were unaware of Edwards’ misconduct.

“There isn’t enough challenge at the top [within the senior leadership team], and there isn’t enough psychological safety among the middle and more junior levels to challenge upwards,” one staff member said, speaking under conditions of anonymity.

  • ICO ‘less effective as a regulator’ due to toxic culture: Staff of the UK’s data protection watchdog say it was ‘less effective’ due to a toxic workplace culture upheld by senior leadership team
  • Former ICO boss found using ‘vulgar’ language with female staff: An independent investigation into UK’s former information commissioner John Edwards uncovers his use of ‘highly sexualised’ language with staff, days after his resignation.
  • UK information commissioner John Edwards resigns after HR investigation: The UK’s information commissioner has resigned following an HR investigation, saying there were occasions when he exercised ‘poor judgement’ and made ‘inappropriate attempts at humour’.
  • ICO strips commissioner Edwards of responsibilities in HR inquiry: The UK’s information commissioner John Edwards has been temporarily stripped of his responsibilities in the wake of a workplace investigation.

Another well-placed anonymous source said: “There’s also a sincerely held belief that complaints about John’s behaviour were not taken forward as they should have been.”

Ken Macdonald, former head of ICO Regions, wrote in a post on LinkedIn today that he was concerned the review is expected to report back by the first quarter of 2027, questioning whether that would leave enough time.

“I fear that’s rather optimistic given the extent of the bullying behaviours which I have been made aware of from some of my former colleagues,” he said. “If proven true … the previous commissioner’s behaviour will be the least of the new commission’s worries.”

Unions campaigned for wider review

The review follows a campaign by staff and trade unions to expand a more limited investigation proposed by the ICO that would have been run internally by the organisation and would have excluded former staff from giving evidence.

The PCS said it had pressed for significant changes, including the appointment of an independent barrister, arrangements for former staff to speak and the ability of the review to scrutinise decisions by managers, following a campaign and a day of action.

General secretary Fran Heathcote said the review was a significant step in addressing longstanding concerns by staff at the ICO. “The review must establish what has gone wrong and deliver meaningful recommendations for change,” she said. “Our members deserve a workplace where bullying and harassment are not tolerated, and nobody is afraid to speak up.”

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, said the review would identify what is working, where things are falling short and what needs to change. “I want current and former staff to feel able to speak openly about their experiences and to know they will be taken seriously,” she said.

Paul Arnold, acting ICO chief executive, said: “While this has been an unsettling time for everyone at the ICO, establishing this independent review in the wake of the former commissioner’s resignation reflects our ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the last year and those leading up to it.”

Former staff signed NDAs

The Information Commission has entered into 16 non-disclosure agreements with current or former members of staff at a cost of £354,000 since January 2020, according to disclosures under the Freedom of Information Act. Nine of the agreements included clauses to prevent employees making disparaging comments about their former employer.

Former technology secretary Kendall told the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee on 8 July that Edwards was “preparing to serve legal papers on one of the women at the ICO who raised concerns about his behaviour”.

Results of staff survey at ICO in May and June 2026

  • Around 63% of respondents say bullying, harassment and discrimination is a serious or very serious problem
  • 50% of respondents say they have been a victim of bullying, harassment and discrimination
  • 75% of respondents do not accept that ICO has a zero-tolerance approach to bullying, harassment and discrimination
  • Around 65% of respondents did not feel confident that complaints are investigated fairly by the ICO
  • 75% of respondents did not believe that perpetrators are held accountable for their actions
  • Only 7% of respondents said that instances of  of bullying, harassment and discrimination were decreasing whilst 93% believed instances were either staying the same or increasing.

Source: FDA

title: Power now the binding constraint on AI datacentres
raw_text:
Europe’s datacentres will more than double electricity demand over the next decade, from about 96TWh (terawatt-hours) in 2024 to around 236TWh by 2035. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence (AI) rack power draw is set to climb steeply, from around 20kW (kilowatts) now to as much as 1MW (megawatt) apiece.

Bring those two trends together and we find the industry – datacentres and their customers – beginning to measure in metrics such as tokens per watt, time to token and cost per token.

That’s according to executives at Schneider Electric’s datacentre event in Conselve, Italy, this week (pictured above), where speakers cited power delivery as key to the AI build-out. The constraint on AI infrastructure, they argued, has moved to electricity – and to how fast it can be delivered.

“We used to talk about a large datacentre if it reached 30MW,” said Damien Dhellemmes, senior vice-president of Schneider Electric’s secure power and datacentre business in Europe. “When you looked at 50MW, it was a big animal in the traditional datacentre world. Now, with AI datacentres – gigafactories – we’re talking hundreds of megawatts and gigawatt campuses.”

Dhellemmes framed the shift around three pressures: time to power, rack density and heat. “We used to talk about 20kW. Now, we’re talking hundreds of kilowatts. Eventually, in one rack you will have up to 1MW,” he said.

Time to power has become the organising principle, said Dhellemmes. “Time to power means time to token, which means time to money. Let’s be straightforward. It is the number one priority and challenge of AI factories,” he said.

From that has come a new set of yardsticks. Andrew Bradner, who leads Schneider’s cooling business, said the industry now talks in a language of its own. “Now we use things like tokens per watt, time to token and cost per token. These measurements talk about how you can be efficient and profitable when you build AI products,” he said.

Tokens per watt measures how much AI work is produced for the energy consumed, while cost per token measures how efficiently that energy converts into usable output.

The engineering response to these metrics is arriving in several forms.

Modular build is one, with Schneider having launched a prefabricated datacentre range called RapidScale while developing an 800V DC “sidecar” to carry power down to the rack.

Grid flexibility is another. Dhellemmes pointed to DCFLEX, an initiative led by the US Electric Power Research Institute, which Schneider joined with more than 40 companies to work out how datacentres can balance supply and demand by, for example, running heavy AI workloads overnight, or returning stored energy from batteries and uninterruptible power supplies to the grid.

Then there is procurement. Silvia Alchini, who leads Schneider’s secure power business in Italy, argued that long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) give operators visibility and a route to new renewables.

“The power purchase agreement, for example, is a long-term agreement in which a company can commit to purchasing renewable energy under defined economic conditions,” she said.

Schneider pointed to a French deal that saw Equinix agree 20-year PPAs for more than 300GWh (gigawatt-hours) a year across wind farms in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, Hauts-de-France and Pays de la Loire, and allocated to 11 French datacentres.

The operator’s view: Europe’s two-speed power market

Liam Newcombe (pictured) is senior vice-president of product, energy strategy and innovation at GreenScale Data Centres, which runs sites in Norway and Northern Ireland. He sees two very different markets.

“The Nordics has a reputation as a green and cheap power market, and much of it is still very green. Our site in Norway, with just a regular grid mix, is around 99% renewable,” he said.

Meanwhile, Northern Ireland has renewable promise but is hamstrung by an inability to keep generating power. “Northern Ireland presents itself as sort of Saudi Arabia of wind,” said Newcombe. “But we still only get about 40% to 45% capacity from wind there, and for the rest of the year, we have to find something else. Unfortunately, on that grid at the moment, a lot of it is gas. We don’t have the depth of storage yet.”

Also, the price gap shocks tenants used to American rates, he said. “When you tell an American tenant they’re going to pay $200-plus a megawatt hour, they look confused because they used to pay $20, $40, $60 a megawatt hour in those markets,” added Newcombe. The fix, he argued, is to put renewables behind the meter and get “the price down to something that’s competitive and effective in terms of tokens per dollar”.

Which leaves the question of where AI actually gets built. For UK IT leaders, power price, not just time to power, influences the map. Behind-the-meter renewables and PPAs are available levers, but situating generation behind the meter runs into planning and community opposition in the UK.

That makes the tokens-per-watt and cost-per-token discipline the thing that separates viable builds from the rest. In a market where power is expensive and slow to connect, projects that survive will be the ones that wring the most AI work from every watt.

Datacentre cooling glossary

PUE (power usage effectiveness): Total facility energy divided by the energy the IT equipment uses. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt reaches the servers; 1.2 means 20% extra goes on cooling, power delivery and losses.

WUE (water usage effectiveness): Water consumed per unit of IT energy, usually litres per kilowatt-hour. It captures water use, not the carbon intensity of the grid.

Cooling: Removing the heat that IT equipment produces so chips stay inside their operating range. Air or liquid carries the heat from the servers to the heat rejection step.

Heat rejection: Where the captured heat leaves the building – to outside air through a chiller or dry cooler, or to water.

CDU (coolant distribution unit): The pump-and-heat-exchanger unit in liquid cooling. It circulates coolant to the cold plates on the chips and separates the server (technology) loop from the building (facility) loop.

Chiller: The machine that removes heat from the water loop. Newer units combine refrigerant-based cooling (a compressor circuit) with water-coil free cooling, so they run the compressor only when the outside air is too warm and switch to water cooling when it is cool enough.

title: Capita CEO goodbye message talks up tech transformation, but AI failure is his legacy
raw_text:
Capita’s outgoing boss championed the company’s tech transformation in a goodbye message to thousands of staff, but his years of work will be remembered for a tech project that went horribly wrong.

Adolfo Hernandez, who stepped down this week under mounting pressure, was tasked with transforming Capita’s delivery model through technology such as artificial intelligence (AI), but he leaves in the wake of a £239m Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) project disaster, with an AI failure at its core, that has put the company’s future in doubt.

In a message to staff, Hernandez talked of Capita’s three-year journey under his leadership towards becoming a “technology-led, AI-enabled business services company”.

“Together, we reset the strategy, built an AI-led operating model with partners including Microsoft, AWS, Salesforce, Databricks, ServiceNow and Snowflake, rebuilt the leadership team, and saw our clients respond, with customer satisfaction at its highest since we began measuring it,” he wrote.

Hernandez outlined successes to thousands of Capita staff in his message: “That was not a small ambition for an organisation of our size and history, and you made it real: in how we work with our clients, in the platforms we’ve built, and in the way you’ve embraced new tools and new ways of working. This team improved renewal and win rates significantly.”

But he will be remembered as the CEO who was in charge when hundreds of civil servants were thrown into financial hardship because the company he led made a botch of their pensions.

Tech disaster

But Hernandez did not ignore this in his goodbye, admitting it had “not got everything right”.

“I know the Civil Service Pension Scheme has asked a great deal of many of you, and I’m grateful to everyone working to restore the service members deserve,” he said.

The contract to administer the pensions of 1.7 million people was supposed to be a flagship project, demonstrating how AI technology could transform pension administration.

Capita was awarded the contract to run the administration of the CSPS in 2023, when the Cabinet Office handed it a seven-year contract worth £239m.

The contract was set to transfer from MyCSP to Capita in December 2025, allowing two years to prepare. However, as reported by Computer Weekly in October 2025, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) warned there was a “real risk” that Capita would not be ready to take over in December. The supplier’s response to that claim was that it was inaccurate and “not reflective of the current state of the transition”.

But that did turn out to be the case, and within weeks of going live, the Cabinet Office appointed a troubleshooter to attempt to avert disaster. But it was too little too late, and disaster did strike.

During a joint PAC and Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC) hearing, PACAC chair Simon Hoare MP reminded Hernandez that the Cabinet Office was told: “The two-year transition period would lead to the digital artificial intelligence revolution to deliver a world-class, world-leading pension service.”

Hoare added: “None of that was met, neither the novel nor the basic.”

Hernandez conceded: “We have not been able to deploy the technology that would allow us to get there.”

Financial trouble

Capita’s recent profit warning, with losses as a result of the failed Civil Service Pension Scheme expected to top £90m, its plunging share price and the need to raise £190m in the first half of next year are signs of a tough year ahead.

Add to this the UK government’s policy to insource more public sector work and the reluctance of ministers to sign off contracts with a firm that is making headlines for all the wrong reasons.

In May, Computer Weekly revealed ministers refused to sign off a £563m contract to Capita because of the CSPS problems. According to sources, Capita was set to be awarded the Learning Frameworks 2.0 contract, which provides access to learning, development and coaching for public sector organisations. It was planned as the replacement for existing learning and development contracts held by KPMG, but the government cancelled the procurement and will bring the service in-house.

MPs of all colours are rounding on Capita over the Synergy Business Process Services contract, which it won in March despite the CSPS problems. They are demanding Capita lose the deal, which, according to the official tender, has an estimated value of around £959m over 10 years. It supports back-office services for the Department for Work and Pensions, the Ministry of Justice, the Home Office, and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.

Capita has already been stripped of a contract to administer the Royal Mail pension scheme, which is being brought in-house after the supplier missed targets.

More pressure will inevitably come as prime minister Andy Burnham’s government policy to “move forward the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation” gathers momentum. Capita is almost solely reliant on UK public sector business.

The government has already said it is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring [the Civil Service] Pension Scheme back in-house”.

MPs of every party now have a line on Capita. Reform UK MP Richard Tice is the latest, who recently brought forward the urgent question in Parliament. He described his concern over a repeat of the collapse of Carillion following news that Hernandez was stepping down at Capita, alongside the profit warning and share price collapse.

Tice said the government should have a “plan B, a plan C and a plan D”, which “might involve ensuring that Capita can merge with another outsourcing company or underwriting the share issue, or it might have to involve taking it in-house”.

title: Cloudera bets on hybrid AI and data sovereignty as Middle East demand accelerates
raw_text:
The growing complexity of enterprise data environments, combined with increasing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and tighter data sovereignty requirements, is reshaping how organisations approach cloud infrastructure. For Cloudera, the answer is to bring cloud-like flexibility to wherever enterprise data resides, rather than requiring organisations to move everything to public cloud environments.

That was the central message at Cloudera’s Evolve26 event in Madrid, where the company presented Anywhere Cloud, its latest step towards a unified hybrid data and AI platform.

The announcement comes as governments and enterprises across the Middle East accelerate investment in AI infrastructure, sovereign cloud capabilities and locally controlled data environments. For Cloudera, these developments offer an opportunity to expand its position in a region where data sovereignty has long been a strategic priority, particularly in financial services and government.

Opening the event, Cloudera chief executive Charles Sansbury highlighted the scale of investment behind the company’s product evolution, revealing it had spent about US$1bn over the past three years through acquisitions and internal development.

“We’ve spent approximately US$1bn to deliver both the evolution of the Cloudera Data Platform, as well as what we’re introducing today: Anywhere Cloud,” he told delegates.

The investment reflects a shift in how Cloudera sees enterprise technology evolving. Rather than assuming that workloads will eventually migrate entirely to public cloud, the company believes hybrid infrastructure will remain a permanent feature of large enterprise IT environments.

“For the largest, most complex organisations in the world, hybrid deployments are not a waypoint along the journey. They’re an endpoint,” the CEO said.

He argued that organisations continue to retain significant amounts of data within their own infrastructure because of security, regulatory and sovereignty requirements.

“The idea that everything should move to the cloud did not win,” he added, pointing to the importance of keeping proprietary data within an organisation’s defined security perimeter while still benefiting from cloud innovation.

Bringing AI to the data

Anywhere Cloud is designed to address this challenge by providing a common management and orchestration layer across public cloud, private cloud, on-premise infrastructure and sovereign environments.

The objective is to give organisations a consistent cloud-like experience, regardless of where their data and workloads are located, and to let them manage data, analytics and AI across different computing environments through a unified control plane.

The platform aims to remove the traditional trade-off between the flexibility of public cloud and the control associated with private infrastructure.

“You shouldn’t have to choose between that convenience, that ease of use from a cloud perspective, and all of the AI innovation that you want,” Sansbury said.

He added that the platform would allow organisations to deploy AI models in the environments they choose, whether public, private or sovereign, while retaining control over their underlying data.

Cloudera’s chief product officer, Leo Brunnick, outlined the technical foundations behind the approach, highlighting the importance of interoperability, modularity and the ability to deploy workloads across different infrastructure environments.

He described a platform designed to work across on-premise infrastructure, private cloud, air-gapped environments, hyperscalers including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, as well as sovereign cloud providers.

However, deployment flexibility alone is not sufficient, he argued. Organisations also need a unified data fabric to manage governance, security and control across their infrastructure.

The architecture is designed to support different technologies and third-party engines, allowing enterprises to integrate existing investments rather than replace their entire technology stack.

Brunnick also highlighted the platform’s modular design, which allows organisations to upgrade individual components without having to undertake a full platform migration.

One of the key propositions is faster deployment. Cloudera estimates that moving from bare-metal infrastructure or virtual machines to operational data services, a process that can traditionally take around 60 days could be reduced to 60 minutes or less through Anywhere Cloud.

The platform also builds on Cloudera’s wider data and AI developments, including its Kona release, which brings together improvements to the Cloudera Data Platform, AI inferencing, agent development, data sharing and lakehouse optimisation.

Cloudera CTO Sergio Gago highlighted the growing role of AI within the company’s data architecture, arguing that inferencing is becoming a horizontal capability rather than an isolated feature.

Through its AI services, organisations can deploy models on their own graphics processing units (GPUs), cloud-based GPUs or a combination of both. Its Agent Studio capabilities also allow enterprises to build and manage AI agents that access corporate data under existing governance policies.

For Middle Eastern organisations, the sovereignty dimension of this strategy is particularly relevant. Governments across the Gulf are investing heavily in digital infrastructure and AI capabilities, while financial institutions and other regulated industries face increasing pressure to ensure sensitive data remains protected and governed according to national requirements.

Marenza Altieri-Douglas, vice-president of sovereign cloud strategy at Cloudera, said that although data sovereignty has become more prominent in European technology discussions in recent years, it has been a long-standing priority in the Middle East.

“Organisations, if you think about financial services or government, have always had the need to be in environments where the data was secure and protected,” she said.

“I’ve been around for some years, and having worked for American companies more or less all my life, when it comes to where the data sits and where the data should be, the Middle East has always been particularly attentive to that.”

She added that Cloudera is looking to expand its network of sovereign infrastructure providers and partnerships to give customers greater flexibility in choosing where their workloads operate.

For Altieri-Douglas, the key is not forcing enterprises into a single infrastructure model, but allowing them to select the environment that best meets the requirements of individual workloads.

“Not necessarily everything, all the data that you have, needs to be sitting in one particular environment. You need to have the choice,” she said.

She explained that Anywhere Cloud was developed to combine the control and security traditionally associated with Cloudera’s on-premise technology with the flexibility and convenience of cloud services.

Cloudera’s historical strength in highly controlled, secure environments had sometimes limited flexibility for customers, she acknowledged. The company’s latest direction is intended to address that limitation. “What if I could have both? What if I can have control without losing control, but I can also have the hybrid situation where I can keep my most critical data, for example, in an air-gapped environment, and I can expose the less critical ones to do some innovation?”

This distinction is particularly important as organisations begin deploying generative and agentic AI across their operations. Altieri-Douglas said enterprises needed greater visibility over where their data resides, who can access it and how it is used by AI models.

She also highlighted Cloudera’s partnership with French AI company Mistral, which is intended to support organisations seeking to deploy AI capabilities while maintaining control over proprietary information.

“The data belongs to the customer. The data doesn’t belong to Cloudera,” she said, stressing the importance of maintaining boundaries around corporate information when using large language models.

Cloudera is also developing partnerships with infrastructure and technology providers, including Nvidia and Vast Data, as part of its wider hybrid ecosystem. Altieri-Douglas, who joined Cloudera in September 2026, highlighted the importance of the Middle East market, explaining that she had prioritised a visit to Dubai because of the level of regional demand.

Financial institutions put hybrid data strategies into practice

The requirements described by Cloudera are already reflected in the technology strategies of major financial institutions in the region. At the Madrid event, representatives from Emirates NBD and Mashreq discussed their experiences with Cloudera’s platform, highlighting the importance of infrastructure modernisation, performance and consistent data governance.

Ali Rey, group head of technology platforms at Emirates NBD, described the bank’s ongoing efforts to modernise its data infrastructure and improve the performance of its workloads. He highlighted the importance of upgrading Cloudera’s Data Platform, adopting container-based infrastructure and introducing AI capabilities to accelerate internal workloads.

The bank has been exploring performance improvements through the use of lower-cost GPUs, with Rey describing gains ranging from double performance to approximately four times performance across certain workloads.

“One of the things we’re doing is upgrading CDP to the new version, running containers, but also enabling AI for all our internal jobs to make them a lot faster,” he said.

Rey also reflected on the complexity of large-scale infrastructure transformations, particularly the migration and upgrading of significant volumes of enterprise data.

He described the challenges of moving approximately two petabytes of data during previous platform upgrades, alongside the testing and migration work required to maintain operational continuity.

However, he argued that subsequent upgrades had become easier as the bank developed more procedures and gained experience.

“As scary and as difficult as it may be, it’s not a safe road. But as long as you have that goal in mind, I think change is important,” he said. “Embrace the change.”

For Gyan Prakash Srivastava, head of data analytics at Mashreq, one of the main lessons from large-scale data transformation programmes is the importance of establishing consistent data governance from the outset.

He highlighted the challenges of maintaining consistency across organisations operating multiple business functions, countries and development teams.

Without a common data governance framework, organisations risk creating fragmented approaches to data quality, ownership, metrics and business definitions.

Srivastava said organisations needed to establish common principles covering data quality, business glossaries, metrics and ownership, ensuring that development teams worked within a consistent framework.

He also warned that inconsistent definitions across business functions could create difficulties when organisations needed to report information to regulators or use data across different departments.

Investing in the next phase of enterprise AI

For Cloudera, the evolution towards a unified hybrid platform is part of a broader effort to position itself at the intersection of enterprise data management, AI and digital sovereignty.

The company’s approximately US$1bn investment over the past three years reflects the scale of its ambition, while its partnerships and sovereign infrastructure strategy are intended to extend the platform’s reach across different markets.

In the Middle East, where governments and financial institutions are investing in AI while maintaining strict requirements around data control, the ability to deploy workloads across multiple environments could become an important differentiator.

The challenge for Cloudera will be translating its technology proposition into measurable business value for organisations managing increasingly complex data estates. As enterprises move from AI experimentation towards production deployments, the question is no longer simply which AI models they can access, but where those models run, what data they can use and how organisations retain control over the entire process.
